summary:
FieldShift is a decision-support model which helps farmers adapt their crop rotations to changing rainfall patterns, water shortages, extreme weather and declining soil health. 
Our current initial version focuses on North Dakota farmers and aids them in comparing crops for their county and planning for a dry, typical, or  wet season. The website allows farmers to pick a county on an interactive map, choose a season, and describe the settings of their farm, and FieldShift returns a ranked list of up to eight crops with their expected yields, estimated sales per acre and yield loss in a dry season. To build it, we combined NASA POWER data (daily weather, satellite rain from GPM IMERG and soil wetness) with USDA county yields from 2001 to 2025 and trained a Random Forest model for each crop. Our project addresses the challenge of adapting agriculture to environmental change by turning complex data into practical information that farmers can use when choosing crops. It helps farmers assess how crops are likely to perform while recognizing that predictions cannot guarantee results. 
Our hope is that FieldShift helps farmers plan ahead for changing rainfall, water shortages and extreme weather, reduce the risk of crop losses, and protect their livelihoods and long term food security.
details:
FieldShift is a user-friendly web app developed for North Dakota farmers to evaluate and compare the crops for their county. The website includes an interactive map and allows farmers to pick a county, choose the season type (dry, typical, or wet), and describe their farm (equipment, water, nearby markets and local prices) or proceed with a pre-defined default one. Afterwards, the website returns a sorted list of up to eight crops with information on the expected yield, estimated sales per acre, yield drop in a dry season, as well as the chosen county’s reported yields since 2001. 

To train the model, we combined NASA POWER data, including daily weather, satellite rain from GPM IMERG and soil wetness with the USDA county yields between 2001 and 2025. We chose a Random Forest regression model, which we trained separately for each crop type and connected the change in yield with the given season’s weather. The output of the typical yield in the app is based on each county’s recent reported yields with the model supplying information on the yield change for different seasons (dry vs wet). 

To evaluate model performance, training was performed on prior years and predictions were run on the following one that the model has not seen before. Across the eight crop types, the mean error is around 14.6%. 

When training our model, we recognized that to forecast the yield for the year ahead, the algorithm required weather information for the full season that was not readily available. To overcome the limitation, we chose to turn it into a feature, allowing farmers to choose the season (wet vs dry) and assess the changes. Turning a pre-determined challenge into our website’s main advantage forms the creativity of our approach. 

Finally, when building FieldShift, our main consideration aside from prediction accuracy was to ensure that the tool would be easily accessible to farmers. We chose to build a website in liu of an app for this exact reason - a farmer can simply go online and run a quick assessment without needing to even set up an account. We also implemented accessibility in building a user-friendly interface that walks the user through running predictions step-by-step, doesn’t require any “text” inputs (aside from typed price boxes) and instead provides options to choose from. The website is also easy to navigate and points out limitations for each prediction, where human input would be most needed. 

FieldShift’s intent is to supply farmers with a quick, easy-to-use tool, which they can implement in agricultural planning. Our website allows them to assess which crop types would hold up best in a case of a dry season, taking into account the exact settings of their farm. Our overall hope is that this user-friendly website will allow farmers to avoid severe crop losses by planning ahead as well as serve as a foundation to initiate conversations between farmers, agronomists, and Extension agents to guide rational agricultural planning for years ahead. The impact of FieldShift is to help farmers adapt their crop choices to changing rainfall patterns, water shortages, and extreme weather, using NASA data that is otherwise difficult for them to access. In future versions, we plan to extend FieldShift to include multi-year crop rotations as well as soil health. 

The tools we used are Python including pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, and matplotlib packages, Jupyter notebook (Google Colab), HTML, CSS, and Javascript for website building with the map drawn as an SVG. The model and website were published as a GitHub repository. We consulted Claude AI by Anthropic to help write code for the notebook and build out the website pages.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (daily weather, soil wetness and solar from MERRA-2 and CERES, satellite rain from GPM IMERG)
projectRefs: US Census Bureau Gazetteer (North Dakota counties)
